In brief

Circe takes place in Dublin's red-light district, which Dubliners knew as Monto (or the Monto) because Montgomery Street ran along its southern edge, just north of the docks. This rough and dangerous area, in which houses of prostitution were tolerated, lay only a few blocks east of Sackville (O'Connell) Street Lower. Joyce calls it "nighttown," which Gifford notes was "slang among Dublin journalists for the late shift on a newspaper." Most of the chapter's action takes place in what Ithaca calls "the disorderly house of Mrs Bella Cohen, 82 Tyrone street, lower." Tyrone was the current name of what had been Mecklenburgh Street—a name that is also used twice in the novel. Coming from the Amiens Street railroad station, Stephen and Lynch enter the area via Mabbot Street. Purdon Street is also mentioned.

At more length

Cyril Pearl observes that in addition to a high number of illegal streetwalkers (586 were arrested in 1904, more than double the rate per capita in London that year), "Dublin had, unlike London, a considerable population of whores who functioned lawfully in brothels" (Dublin in Bloomtime, 10). He quotes from the Encyclopaedia Britannica: "Dublin seems to form an exception to the usual practice in the United Kingdom. In that city police permit open brothels confined to one area, but carried on more openly than in the South of Europe or even Algiers" (10). Houses ran the gamut from genteel to shabby: "There were sharp class distinctions in Monto. The most select part was the upper end of Tyrone Street, where the Georgian houses retained some of their elegance and the whores wore fashionable evening dress and were visited regularly by their couturier. Less fastidious were their sisters at the lower end, and in Mabbot Street and Faithful Place, who wore only raincoats which they flicked open occasionally to stimulate trade. In these humbler establishments, 'coshes' of lead pipe were often concealed behind the gaudy religious pictures that brightened the walls" (11).

In Scylla and Charybdis Mulligan recalls finding Stephen on Tyrone Street Upper: "I called upon the bard Kinch at his summer residence in upper Mecklenburgh street and found him deep in the study of the Summa contra Gentiles in the company of two gonorrheal ladies, Fresh Nelly and Rosalie, the coalquay whore." Lynch makes the same connection between this street and Stephen's conversational habits as he and Stephen enter the area in Circe: "Pornosophical philotheology. Metaphysics in Mecklenburgh street!" The two men are entering via "The Mabbot street entrance of nighttown," walking north from the Amiens Street railroad station and heading for Mecklenburgh. They end up at Bella Cohen's house, which does not seem very fancy.

The red-light district serviced many British soldiers, and in 1925, shortly after independence, it was eliminated. The area has gone through many changes subsequently, and streets have been renamed. Montgomery Street is now Foley Street. Mecklenburgh/Tyrone has become Railway Street. Mabbot Street became Corporation Street and then, in 1965, it was renamed James Joyce Street.

John Hunt 2014
